messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

*   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8 \text{ V}$ (settled)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6 \text{ V}$
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05 \text{ V}$
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4 \text{ s}$ (cold start)
        *   $dv \le 0.02 \text{ V}$ (settled stability)
    *   Piezo: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $20\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} \approx 0.76 \text{ V}$ peak (S1). This is very low.
    *   Reference Design (Full Bridge Rectifier - FBR) failed because the output voltage ($0.3\text{--}0.5\text{ V}$) was too low to reach $1.8\text{ V}$, except for S3 (strong excitation).

    *   The piezo voltage is too low for a simple passive rectifier.
    *   To get $1.8\text{ V}$ from a source with a $0.76\text{ V}$ open-circuit peak, we need a DC-DC boost mechanism.
    *   Standard approach for piezo energy harvesting: Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) or a boosted version of it.
    *   SSHI works by flipping the voltage across the piezo capacitor $C_p$ at the peaks of the displacement, effectively multiplying the voltage.
    *   Specifically, the "Parallel SSHI" (P-SSHI) or a switched-capacitor/inductor boost.

    *   *Concept:* Use an inductor and a switch to invert the charge on $C_p$ when the voltage reaches a peak.
    *   *Basic SSHI cycle:*
        1. Piezo charges $C_p$ and the storage cap $C_{out}$ through a rectifier.
        2. When $V_{pzp}$ reaches a peak, a switch closes across $C_p$ (via an inductor) to flip its polarity.
    *   Wait, the reference design results show that even with a full bridge, we aren't hitting $1.8\text{ V}$. The open-circuit voltage is too low.
    *   The standard SSHI topology usually involves a rectifier and a switch that shorts the piezo through an inductor at the peaks.

    *   *Topology 1: P-SSHI (Parallel SSHI)*
        *   Rectifier (Full Bridge) to charge $C_{out}$.
        *   Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
        *   The switch $S$ closes at the peaks to flip the voltage across $C_p$.
        *   This increases the voltage available to the rectifier.
        *   Wait, if the switch $S$ is across $C_p$, the current goes $C_p \to L \to C_p$. This flips the voltage.
        *   Actually, the most common efficient topology for low-voltage piezo is the "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE) or SSHI. Let's try a simplified SSHI.

    *   *Topology 2: SSHI with an active boost/step-up.*
        *   Since $V_{oc}$ is only $0.76 \text{ V}$, and the load needs $1.8 \text{ V}$, we really need a voltage multiplier or a boost.
        *   Let's consider a "Boost" converter where the piezo charges a capacitor, and then a switch-inductor combination kicks it up. But the piezo is an AC source.

    *   *Topology 3: Inductive Boost (Standard SSHI)*
        *   Components: Full Bridge (4 x DSCH), an inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo terminals (pzp, pzn).
        *   SYNC controller: `edges: "both"`, `ton` set to the resonant period $\pi \sqrt{LC_p}$.
        *   This flips the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively adding the flipped voltage to the next half-cycle, increasing the voltage seen by the bridge.

    *   $C_p = 25 \text{ nF}$
    *   $f = 100 \text{ Hz}$
    *   $L$ needs to be chosen such that $\pi \sqrt{LC_p}$ is small (e.g., $10\text{--}100 \mu\text{s}$).
    *   $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{0.001 \times 25\text{e-9}} \approx 15.7 \mu\text{s}$. This is within the SYNC range ($1\text{e-07}$ to $0.001$).
    *   $C_{out}$ needs to be large enough to keep ripple low ($0.05 \text{ V}$).

    *   Rectifier:
        *   D1: [pzp, out]
        *   D2: [pzn, out]
        *   D3: [0, pzp]
        *   D4: [0, pzn]
        *   Actually, standard full bridge:
            D1: [pzp, out]
            D2: [pzn, out]
            D3: [0, pzp] (No, this is wrong).
            Correct Full Bridge:
            D1: [pzp, out]
            D2: [pzn, out]
            D3: [0, pzp] (Wait, the provided reference bridge is: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]. Let's re-examine that:
            D1: pzp -> out
            D2: pzn -> out
            D3: 0 -> pzp
            D4: 0 -> pzn
            If $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$, D1 conducts. Current: $pzp \to out \to 0 \to pzn$.
            If $V_{pzn} > V_{out}$, D2 conducts. Current: $pzn \to out \to 0 \to pzp$.
            This is a valid bridge if the source is between pzp and pzn.
    *   SSHI part:
        *   Inductor L1: [pzp, n1]
        *   Switch S1: [n1, pzn]
        *   SYNC G1: `edges: "both"`, `ton` approx $15 \mu\text{s}$.

    *   Can we do better? A Zener clamp on "out" is needed to ensure $v_{max} \le 3.6 \text{ V}$.
    *   DZ33 is a 3.3V Zener.
    *   D_clamp: [0, out], model DZ33.

    *   Wait, SSHI usually increases the voltage across the piezo. If the open circuit voltage is $0.76\text{ V}$, flipping the voltage might get us closer to $1.5\text{--}2\text{ V}$. But the diode drops (0.25V x 2 = 0.5V) might still be too high.
    *   Actually, if we use SSHI, the voltage across the piezo peaks at $V_{piezo} = \frac{2}{\pi} \frac{I_p}{f C_p} \times \text{gain}$.
    *   Let's refine the P-SSHI:
        Full Bridge (DSCH)
        L1 from pzp to n1, S1 from n1 to pzn.
        G1 SYNC (edges: both, ton: 20us).
        C_out on out.
        D_zener on out.

    *   S1: $V_{oc} = 0.76 \text{ V}$. With $V_{drop} = 0.5 \text{ V}$, the output $V_{out} \approx 0.26 \text{ V}$.
    *   SSHI (Parallel) can increase the voltage across the capacitor $C_p$. The theoretical maximum voltage across $C_p$ with SSHI is $V_{p,max} \approx \frac{I_p}{\pi f C_p} \times \text{some factor}$.
    *   Wait, the reference design (FBR) failed on S1 with $v_{avg} = 0.56 \text{ V}$. This means the $V_{oc}$ isn't actually the limiting factor in the way I thought, but the voltage is simply too low to reach $1.8 \text{ V}$ given the load $R_L = 10\text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   Wait, $v_{avg} = 0.56 \text{ V}$ for $R_L = 10\text{ M}\Omega$ means $P_{load} = 0.56^2 / 10\text{e6} = 31 \text{ nW}$.
    *   The required $v_{avg} \ge 1.8 \text{ V}$ for $R_L = 10\text{ M}\Omega$ requires $P_{load} = 1.8^2 / 10\text{e6} = 324 \text{ nW}$.
    *   The energy harvested is $P_{avg} \approx \frac{I_p^2}{2 \pi f C_p}$ ? No, that's not right.
    *   For a piezo, $P_{max} = \frac{I_p^2}{2 \pi f C_p} \dots$ No.
    *   Actually, the maximum power a piezo can deliver is $P_{max} = \frac{(V_{oc,peak})^2}{2 R_{opt}}$? No.
    *   Let's use the current $I_p$. The energy per half cycle is $\frac{1}{2} C_p V_{peak}^2$.
    *   If we use SSHI, we can extract more energy.

    *   What about a Charge Pump? A piezo can drive a charge pump.
    *   But with $V_{oc} = 0.76 \text{ V}$, a charge pump would need many stages.
    *   Let's stick to SSHI first as it's the gold standard for piezo.

    *   $C_p = 25 \text{ nF}$
    *   $L = 1 \text{ mH}$
    *   $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{1\text{e-3} \times 25\text{e-9}} = 15.7 \mu\text{s}$.
    *   $C_{out} = 10 \mu\text{F}$ (to keep ripple low).
    *   $D_{zener}$ = DZ33.

    *   Is there any other topology?
    *   Maybe a "Cold Start" friendly boost?
    *   The SYNC controller is "ideal," meaning it doesn't need $V_{out}$ to operate (though it draws $0.5 \mu\text{A}$ from it). This is a huge advantage.

    *   Let's try three variations:
        1.  P-SSHI (Parallel SSHI) with a full bridge.
        2.  P-SSHI but with a half-bridge (if that's possible/better).
        3.  A different SSHI variant or a simple boost.

    *   Wait, let's refine the "Parallel SSHI" (P-SSHI).
        The switch $S$ is in parallel with the piezo.
        Rectifier: 4 diodes.
        $C_{out}$ and $D_{zener}$.

    *   Is there any risk of $v_{max} > 3.6 \text{ V}$?
        S3 has strong excitation ($I_p = 40 \mu\text{A}$). SSHI might push $V_{out}$ too high.
        The DZ33 zener clamp is essential.

    *   Wait, I should check the `ton` for different $L$.
        If $L = 4.7 \text{ mH}$, $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{4.7\text{e-3} \times 25\text{e-9}} \approx 34 \mu\text{s}$.
        If $L = 10 \text{ mH}$, $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{10\text{e-3} \times 25\text{e-9}} \approx 50 \mu\text{s}$.

    *   Let's try:
        Design 1: P-SSHI (Full Bridge, $L=1\text{mH}$, $C_{out}=10\mu\text{F}$, Zener)
        Design 2: P-SSHI (Full Bridge, $L=10\text{mH}$, $C_{out}=10\mu\text{F}$, Zener)
        Design 3: SSHI with a different switch configuration (though Parallel is usually best). Let's try one with a slightly different $C_{out}$ or different diode models. Actually, let's try a "half-wave" SSHI to see if it's more efficient (though unlikely). Or better, a different $t_{on}$/L combination.

    *   Wait, the prompt says "propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures)".
        L=1mH and L=10mH are the same structure.
        So I need different topologies.

    *   *Topology 1: Parallel SSHI (P-SSHI)*
        - Full bridge (4 diodes)
        - $L$ and $S$ in parallel with piezo
        - $C_{out}$ and $D_{zener}$

    *   *Topology 2: Series SSHI (S-SSHI)*
        - In S-SSHI, the inductor and switch are in series with the piezo.
        - This is more complex. Let's try a "Charge-Pump" like structure?
        - Or a "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE) circuit.
        - SECE: Piezo $\to$ Switch $\to$ Inductor $\to$ Rectifier.
        - In SECE, the piezo is open-circuit during the charging phase and then connected to the storage cap via an inductor at the peak.

    *   *Topology 3: Simple Boost (L-C-S)*
        - This is usually for DC. For AC, we need the rectifier first.
        - What if we put the inductor *before* the rectifier?
        - Piezo $\to$ L $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ $C_{out}$.
        - This is just a filter.

    *   Let's reconsider the SECE topology:
        1. Piezo (pzp, pzn) charges an internal capacitor $C_{int}$ (which is $C_p$ itself).
        2. At the peak, a switch $S$ connects $C_p$ to $L$, and $L$ is connected to the rectifier.
        3. This allows the energy to be transferred more efficiently.

    *   Let's refine P-SSHI (Topology 1) and then think of Topology 2.
        P-SSHI:
        D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn]
        L1: [pzp, n1], S1: [n1, pzn], G1: [SYNC]
        C1: [out, 0]
        DZ1: [0, out] (model DZ33)

    *   Topology 2: SECE (Simplified)
        The piezo charges $C_p$. At the peak, we switch the piezo to an inductor that then feeds the storage cap.
        Wait, a simpler version of SECE:
        S1: [pzp, n1], G1: [SYNC, edges: "pos"]
        L1: [n1, out]
        D1: [out, n1] (to allow current to flow into out)
        This is getting complicated. Let's try a more robust P-SSHI.

    *   Topology 3: A "Voltage Doubler" or "Greinacher" circuit.
        These are passive. Given the $V_{oc} = 0.76 \text{ V}$, a doubler might get us to $1.5 \text{ V}$, but not $1.8 \text{ V}$ after diode drops.

    *   Let's focus on the P-SSHI. Is there any other way to improve it?
        What if we use a "Synchronous" rectifier? (Using switches instead of diodes).
        The SYNC controller can only handle 2 controllers and 4 switches.
        We can use 2 switches for the rectifier and 1 for the SSHI flip.
        Wait, the SYNC can track the frequency and provide pulses.
        If we use switches for the rectifier, we can eliminate the 0.5V diode drop.

    *   *Topology 2: Synchronous Rectifier SSHI*
        - S1: [pzp, out], ctrl: G1 (edges: "pos", phase: 0)
        - S2: [pzn, out], ctrl: G2 (edges: "neg", phase: 0)
        - S3: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1 (edges: "both", ton: 20us) -- this is getting messy.
        - Let's use the SYNC controllers wisely.
        - G1: edges: "both", ton: 20us, phase: 0 (for the SSHI flip).
        - G2: edges: "both", ton: 0.001 (for the rectifier).
        - Wait, a synchronous rectifier needs to be closed for half the period, not $1\text{ms}$.
        - `ton` max is 0.001s. At 100Hz, the period is 0.01s. So $t_{on}$ cannot cover the whole half-period (0.005s).
        - So synchronous rectification is not possible with the given `ton` limit.

    *   *Topology 2: P-SSHI with different rectifier.*
        Wait, the reference FBR is:
        D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn]
        This is basically a bridge.
        What if we use a different inductor position?
        L1: [pzp, out], S1: [out, pzn]? No.

    *   Let's try a "Half-Bridge SSHI" (H-SSHI).
        Pzn is connected to 0.
        D1: [pzp, out]
        L1: [pzp, n1], S1: [n1, 0]
        This only works for one half-cycle.

    *   Let's go back to the P-SSHI and try different variations of it.
        Actually, let's try a *Boost Converter* topology.
        Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ C_intermediate $\to$ Boost (L, S, D) $\to$ C_out.
        1. Rectifier: D1..D4, C_int: [n_int, 0].
        2. Boost: L1: [n_int, n2], S1: [n2, 0], D5: [n2, out], C_out: [out, 0].
        3. G1: SYNC, edges: "both", ton: 20us.
        This would definitely boost the voltage.

    *   Let's refine the Boost Topology:
        D1: [pzp, n_int], D2: [pzn, n_int], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn]
        C_int: [n_int, 0]
        L1: [n_int, n2]
        S1: [n2, 0], ctrl: G1
        D5: [n2, out]
        C_out: [out, 0]
        G1: SYNC, edges: "both", ton: 20us, phase: 0.
        D_zener: [0, out]

    *   P-SSHI: Rectifier is *after* the SSHI flip.
        - Piezo is flipped by L-S.
        - Current is then rectified by the bridge.
        - This increases the voltage across the piezo, thus increasing the voltage at the rectifier's input.
    *   Boost: Rectifier is *before* the boost.
        - Piezo is rectified to a low DC voltage.
        - This DC voltage is then boosted by the L-S-D boost converter.

    *   Which is better?
        - P-SSHI is specifically designed for piezo and is generally more efficient.
        - Boost converter is a general DC-DC.
        - Given the very low $V_{oc}$, a boost converter might struggle to start (cold start) because the $V_{int}$ will be very low ($0.5\text{ V}$), and the boost converter needs some voltage to operate. But the SYNC controller is ideal, so it can switch regardless.

    *   P-SSHI:
        D1: [pzp, out], D2: [pzn, out], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn]
        L1: [pzp, n1], S1: [n1, pzn], G1: SYNC(both, ton: 20us)
        C1: [out, 0]
        D_zener: [0, out]

    *   Boost:
        D1: [pzp, n1], D2: [pzn, n1], D3: [0, pzp], D4: [0, pzn]
        C1: [n1, 0]
        L1: [n1, n2], S1: [n2, 0], G1: SYNC(both, ton: 20us)
        D5: [n2, out]
        C2: [out, 0]
        D_zener: [0, out]

    *   Is there a third?
        Let's try a "Charge Pump" if possible, but that requires more switches.
        What if we use a simpler SSHI (without the full bridge, just a half bridge and a cap)?
        Or maybe a "Series SSHI"?
        S-SSHI:
        L1: [pzp, n1], S1: [n1, out], G1: SYNC.
        Wait, the P-SSHI is the most reliable. Let's try a P-SSHI with different $C_{out}$ or $L$.
        But wait, I need different *connectivity*.
        How about a P-SSHI but with a *capacitor* instead of an *inductor* for the flip? (Switched-capacitor).
        S1: [pzp, n1], S2: [n1, pzn]. This doesn't flip the voltage.
        S1: [pzp, n1], S2: [n1, pzn], and a cap $C_{flip}$... too many switches.

    *   Let's try a "Voltage Doubler" for Topology 3.
        C1: [pzp, n1]
        D1: [n1, out]
        D2: [pzp, 0]
        C2: [out, 0]
        This is a basic doubler. Not very efficient.

    *   Let's go with:
        1. P-SSHI (Parallel SSHI with Full Bridge)
        2. Boost (Rectifier followed by Boost Converter)
        3. SECE-like (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction - simplified)
